lessonRef.subject: financial-literacy
lessonRef.title: Application or project: secured and unsecured debt

objective: Learners analyze two fictional simulated borrowing situations, one backed by collateral (secured) and one not (unsecured), identify which is which, and explain what the lender could do in each situation if the fictional borrower stopped paying.
scenario: This is a fictional, simulated scenario with no real loan, lender, or account involved: two made-up situations describe how two fictional people borrow money and what backs each loan.
materials: the two fictional borrowing situations on this task sheet

tasks.directions: Fictional Situation A: Rosa borrows simulated money to buy a bicycle. If she stops paying, the fictional lender can take the bicycle back.

prompts.text: Is Situation A a secured or unsecured debt?
Name the specific item that backs, or secures, this fictional loan.

tasks.directions: Fictional Situation B: Jamal borrows simulated money using a card with no specific item backing it. If he stops paying, the fictional lender cannot automatically take any of his belongings; it must pursue other collection steps.

prompts.text: Is Situation B a secured or unsecured debt?
Explain the one specific difference between Situation A and Situation B that determines which is secured.

tasks.directions: Think about risk to the lender in each situation.

prompts.text: Which situation is generally riskier for the lender if the fictional borrower stops paying?
Explain your risk answer using what backs, or does not back, each loan.
Based on what you know about risk and interest from this unit, explain which type of debt, secured or unsecured, you would expect to typically carry a higher interest rate, and why.

remediation: If a learner confuses secured and unsecured, reteach with a single memorable rule: secured means something specific backs it up and can be taken back; unsecured means nothing specific backs it, only a promise to pay. Apply the rule to two new one-sentence situations before returning to the original two.
extension: Have the learner write one new fictional borrowing situation of their own, either secured or unsecured, and explain which type it is and what specific item, if any, backs it.
